sents.text: On a server, there's no mouse and no desktop.
You talk to the computer through the terminal: you type a command, press Enter, and it answers in text.
It looks old-fashioned, but it's fast and exact, and it works the same on your laptop, in Colab, or on a GPU server on the other side of the world.
Every command has the same shape.
First the command itself: the action.
Then options, which start with a dash and change how it behaves.
Then arguments: what to act on, like a folder or a file.
So ls, dash l, slash content means: list, in long form, the folder called content.
You don't need to install anything.
The Colab notebook from Lesson three already runs on a Linux computer.
In a code cell, start a line with an exclamation mark, and Colab sends it to Linux instead of Python.
Try exclamation pwd, and exclamation whoami.
pwd prints the working directory: where you are.
And whoami tells you which user you are.
In Colab, whoami answers root: the all-powerful administrator.
We'll see why that matters in the lesson on sudo.
